query: For high-entropy-alloy coatings used in wear-resistant applications, what single intervention could improve wear resistance across operating temperatures? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise identical unmodified coating, the temperature and sliding conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of titanium to high-entropy-alloy coatings will improve wear resistance across operating temperatures.
generation.intervention: Addition of titanium to the alloy
generation.conditions: Operating temperatures above 800 °C, sliding conditions with increased load and velocity
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of solid-solution strengthening and precipitated intermetallic compound phases
generation.mechanism: Dispersion strengthening mechanism, where titanium causes solid-solution strengthening and the formation of brittle phases, leading to increased strength and hardness
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance, with a potential 10-fold improvement over steel substrates
generation.boundary: Operating temperatures below 800 °C, sliding conditions with low load and velocity
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of titanium required for optimal wear resistance, and the potential for introducing cracks and defects during the laser cladding process

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear test with varying titanium content and operating temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear rate of the titanium-modified coating is not significantly lower than the unmodified coating at operating temperatures above 800 °C, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most investigated HEA systems is AlCoCrCuFeNi and the copper-free derivate AlCoCrFeNi [,]. Distinct improvement of mechanical properties can be achieved by alloying with titanium. Due to its large atomic radius, the addition of titanium causes solid–solution strengthening and hence increased strength and hardness. Additionally, the formation of brittle phases was observed for a high content of titanium [,,]. The wear resistance of the alloy system AlCoCrFeNiTi has been investigated under various conditions revealing an increased wear resistance, also in comparison with the steels EN 1.3505 and EN 1.3343 [,]. Although improved high-temperature properties of AlCoCrFeNiTi are expected, the wear behaviour has not yet been investigated at increased temperature.

The investigations prove the suitability of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 for high temperature applications. Due to the formation of protective oxides, an improvement of wear behaviour occurs. Further investigations have to be conducted to determine the wear behaviour under different wear conditions. The influence of the additional σ-phase has to be investigated in subsequent studies.

HEA are a class of materials that contain 5–13 principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions; they have attracted a wide range of interesting research due to their excellent mechanical properties []. In recent years, a variety of HEA were reported publicly in the literature [,,,,]. Among them, AlCoCrFeNi HEA composed of a single BCC solid solution phase shows excellent corrosion resistance and has great potential for surface coating applications [,,,,,]. However, an insufficient high temperature wear-resistance of AlCoCrFeNi HEA greatly limits their practical applications at elevated temperatures (above 800 °C). According to the principle of dispersion strength, the strength and hardness of the simple solid solution phases could be improved further by the precipitated intermetallic compound phases. From the perspective of the dispersion strengthening mechanism, WC, TiC ceramic particles are commonly used as reinforcement phases in high-entropy alloys [,,]. These granular-shaped precipitates can improve the microhardness and wear resistance of the coating.
